newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian retailers need consolidation to grow - DBRS.
newsitem.headline: Canadian retailers need consolidation to grow - DBRS.

text.p: Canada's retail industry needs more downsizing to give retailers room to expand after the influx of competitive U.S. retailers in recent years, said a study by Dominion Bond Rating Service released this week.

"DBRS considers that there are still too many retailers competing in Canada, and that some form of industry consolidation is necessary to restore profitability and put Canadian retailing on a sound footing for growth," the Toronto-based service found.
If not, retailers will see profits capped at recent levels, the study said.

"Unless there are further bankruptcies, closures, or industry consolidation through mergers or acquisitions, longer-term profitability for most retailers in Canada is likely to be restrained," the study found.
"Unless and until that occurs, many of Canada's merchandisers are likely to show below average performance, except for some of the speciality retailers," it said.
Wal-Mart Canada, a subdiary of Wal-Mart Stores Inc has operated at gross margins of 26-30 percent.
This has forced Canadians chains like Hudson's Bay Co unit Zellers to drop prices to compete.

Before Wal-Mart came to Canada in the spring of 1994, discount department stores had a gross margin of 30-35 percent, while senior department stores such as The Bay operated at margins of 35-40 percent.
Despite the gloomy prognosis, DBRS found some positive trends for 1997.
"After a severe product price war in 1994-1995...there has been a trend in 1996 towards higher prices and, therefore, higher operating margins," it said.

Other positive signs include a slow-down in Canadian retail bankruptcies in 1996, the limited creation of new retail space as real estate developers try to improve weakened balance sheets and a recovery in the housing industry compared to last year's dismal numbers, the study said.
